I basically no lifed this game for a day and understood how to type porthack multiple times in a row.

if you want to get into linux (or python???) then this is a good starting point, the 'hacking tools' arent real but commands like ls cd rm are actually used irl and this way you get comfortable with them.

i do recommend to play this game if your knowledge is 0 but its also fun to test your knowledge if you are skilled.

As a console nerd myself the simulated networking and CLI is really cool. I wouldn't say its a "way to learn hacking" as some youtubers have. But it is the closest game I have ever played that really simulates hacking in any way. As someone who actually knows the terminal/console in and out and has a 25 foot long .bashrc with 5 feet of aliases in it I will say that learning the specific command line arguments the game uses were super frustrating because I kept trying to use tools that were not there or using syntax the game didn't like. In a way that's what it IS like for a beginner so that's pretty cool. Also, real hacking often drops you into minimalist server/controller environments where you also may not have tools you expect so overall I found it really dope. 

due props to the devs.

This game, to me, was an absolute MASTERPIECE from start to finish. As someone who is pretty much compsci inept, bar the obligatory "hello world" Python script, this game absolutely hooked me in from the first contract. The tools used within the game are explained perfectly and are not complex; even someone like me felt like the typical underground hacker featured in a 90s movie, typing across 5 different keyboards after 30 minutes of solid gameplay. Once you've used the mechanics a couple of times, it becomes second nature to know when to use them and why. After that, you pick up on the subtle ways to sequence your commands to absolutely speedrun other systems. IMO it's even cooler that it teaches you actual Linux commands (from someone who's never gone near that OS, I had a little giddy moment when I realised that).
The base game features an excellent storyline that evoked real emotion upon completion. I was immersed to the point of feeling the relief, satisfaction, pride, and bittersweetness provoked by how this game concludes Bit's chapter.
An immense thank you to the dev team for making me fall in love with a game so out of my normal genres. Hacknet was an experience. One that I will want to replay again and again if only to hear that ending clip once more. It's insane to think something released just over a decade ago holds up so incredibly well today. The hard work put into every moment of this title, truly, still shines through today.

Anyone scrolling through reviews contemplating it, BUY IT! You will NOT regret it

This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. The tutorial got me curious enough with the plot to get through, but there is no substance in the base game. Haven't played the DLC, not interested.

If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). There are no puzzles, the exploits are literal executables you run and wait, the only variability is whether the target machine has proxies or a firewall then you gotta login into a bunch of places you already hacked first and run a shell overload (run and wait) then run a firewall analyzer to unscramble a keyword (run and read). Sometimes you gotta disconnect before a tracing timer runs out, which is never an issue until a single mission has like a 3 seconds timer but same difference. If you do *somehow* get traced, you might need to do the one different thing and change your IP address by... following steps 1 through 6! Or just reboot. Yeah, that's it: steps 1-7, sprinkle disconnects according to timer and if something fails just reboot and resume as usual is the whole game. There are two routes if you accept an optional mission but rest assured, same gameplay eveywhere.

All around a beautifully simplistic premise with some quality attention to detail; one of the most immersive game experiences I've had in the last decade. One particular mission (you'll know which one) had me genuinely considering the option to refuse it, and had me sit for 10 minutes afterwards processing the result of going through with it.

9/10: easily an experience I would recommend to anyone. Still breaks my heart to this day that the Multiplayer development was scrapped.

Hacknet offers a surprisingly realistic experience of hacking through a command-line interface. I really appreciated how immersive and educational it was, especially for those interested in cybersecurity or Linux-style environments. The game does a great job simulating real-world hacking concepts, making it both fun and intellectually engaging.

However, some of the tools and techniques used in the game are starting to feel outdated. It would be great to see an update or expansion that introduces more current hacking tools and methods, especially as the field continues to evolve quickly.

Overall, I definitely recommend Hacknet to anyone curious about ethical hacking or looking for a unique puzzle game. A modern refresh would make it even better!

narrative puzzle game disguised as a hacker sim, but said narrative is extremely captivating.  worth a playthrough if you're even slightly interested from what you've seen on the store page.

highly reminiscent of uplink, but with more emphasis on knowing command line as opposed to managing a GUI of apps.  no permadeath like in uplink, and some scenarios that happen in uplink that would've resulted in your save being nuked are intentional and part of the narrative/gameplay.  some commands in-game are aliased to similar real life counterparts (the port "probe" command can be executed with "nmap") which is cute.

there are some issues, such as the aforementioned aliases not working fully for other commands, tab completion not being fully implemented (cannot tab complete folder paths, just command names), folder paths from root don't start with a trailing slash, which results in strange behaviour (and makes moving files frustrating!), and from what i've seen around the forums and steam discussions for this game, there are quite a few unpatched game breaking bugs.  the game is also starting to have trouble on modern systems (it is 10 years old!), so i'd say give it a playthrough before it becomes any harder to run.  windows version works great, mac version freezes up after a couple minutes of gameplay on apple silicon-based macs, but theoretically should still work great on intel currently, and have not tried linux version yet myself, but know friends who had a great crash free experience on there.

if you finish the base game and DLC wanting more (very likely scenario) there is a mod scene for the game (both steam workshop and outside the workshop) where many people have created new hack types, new entire scenarios to go through, and at time of writing there is an archipelago multiworld integration in the works, so you'll be able to get more hacknet in your blood stream someway.  favourite game i slept on.
